   162	  // ==== zip(a, b) — parallel iterable of pairs, truncating to the shorter =====
   163	  rule applyBuiltin("zip", list(A:ValSeq), list(B:ValSeq), .Vals) => zipObj(A, B)
   164	  rule applyBuiltin("zip", str(A:IntSeq), str(B:IntSeq), .Vals)   => zipObjS(A, B)
   165	
   166	  // zip's iterator-protocol cases (zip is created here, so its #iterNext lives here)
   167	  rule <k> #iterNext(zipObj(vCons(A:Val, As:ValSeq), vCons(B:Val, Bs:ValSeq)))
   168	        => #iterYield(tuple(vCons(A, vCons(B, .ValSeq))), zipObj(As, Bs)) ... </k>
   169	  rule <k> #iterNext(zipObj(.ValSeq, _:ValSeq))               => #iterDone ... </k>
   170	  rule <k> #iterNext(zipObj(vCons(_:Val, _:ValSeq), .ValSeq)) => #iterDone ... </k>
   171	  rule <k> #iterNext(zipObjS(iCons(A:Int, As:IntSeq), iCons(B:Int, Bs:IntSeq)))
   172	        => #iterYield(tuple(vCons(str(iCons(A, .IntSeq)), vCons(str(iCons(B, .IntSeq)), .ValSeq))), zipObjS(As, Bs)) ... </k>
   173	  rule <k> #iterNext(zipObjS(.IntSeq, _:IntSeq))              => #iterDone ... </k>
   174	  rule <k> #iterNext(zipObjS(iCons(_:Int, _:IntSeq), .IntSeq)) => #iterDone ... </k>
   175	
   176	  // ==== range(stop) / range(start, stop) / range(start, stop, step) =========
   177	  rule applyBuiltin("range", I:Int, .Vals)               => rangeObj(0, I, 1)
   178	  rule applyBuiltin("range", A:Int, B:Int, .Vals)        => rangeObj(A, B, 1)
   179	  rule applyBuiltin("range", A:Int, B:Int, S:Int, .Vals) => rangeObj(A, B, S)
   180	       requires S =/=Int 0
   181	
   182	  // ==== eval(str) — arithmetic expressions (ints, + - * // **, spaces) ========
   183	  // Python precedence: ** right-assoc, then * //, then + -. Promoted from 160's
   184	  // trusted pass evaluator, now DEFINED in the reference and driven by a
   185	  // code-level tokenizer. Reduces on concrete strings (krun); a symbolic
   186	  // argument leaves the call unevaluated for problem-level folds.
   187	  rule applyBuiltin("eval", str(CS:IntSeq), .Vals) => evalArith(CS)
   188	  syntax Int ::= evalArith(IntSeq) [function]
   189	  rule evalArith(CS:IntSeq)
   190	    => firstNdE(passAddE(passMulE(passPowE(tokOps(CS), tokNds(CS)))))
     1	// reference/src/semantics/subscript.k — MPY-SUBSCRIPT
     2	
     3	module MPY-SUBSCRIPT
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	
     6	  // ==== positional access + negative-index normalization (used only here) ===
     7	  // valSeqAt is [total]: in-bounds vCons access reduces as usual; on an OPAQUE sequence (e.g.
     8	  // a trusted sort's sortVS(VS)) or OOB it stays an abstract total value — so indexing the
     9	  // opaque sorted list is DEFINED (no undischarged #Ceil), matching the old semantics' total
    10	  // atK. K trusts the [total] annotation; valid programs index in-bounds.
    11	  syntax Val ::= valSeqAt(ValSeq, Int) [function, total]
    12	  rule valSeqAt(vCons(V:Val, _:ValSeq), 0)     => V
    13	  rule valSeqAt(vCons(_:Val, S:ValSeq), I:Int) => valSeqAt(S, I -Int 1)
    14	       requires I >Int 0
    15	
    16	  syntax Int ::= intSeqAt(IntSeq, Int) [function]
    17	  rule intSeqAt(iCons(C:Int, _:IntSeq), 0)     => C
    18	  rule intSeqAt(iCons(_:Int, S:IntSeq), I:Int) => intSeqAt(S, I -Int 1)
    19	       requires I >Int 0
    20	
    21	  syntax Int ::= normIdx(Int, Int) [function, total]
    22	  rule normIdx(I:Int, LEN:Int) => I +Int LEN requires I  <Int 0
    23	  rule normIdx(I:Int, _:Int)   => I          requires I >=Int 0
    24	
    25	  // ==== Subscript: indexing obj[i] (list / tuple / str) =====================
    26	  // contexts (not strict attrs): the Index slot's Slice alternative must never heat
    27	  context Subscript(HOLE, _)
    28	  context Subscript(_:Val, HOLE:Expr)
    29	
    30	  // heap-object deref (covers both the index and slice forms via the Index slot)
    31	  rule <k> Subscript(ref(H:Int), IX:Index) => Subscript(V, IX) ... </k>
    32	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    33	       [priority(40)]
    34	
    35	  rule <k> Subscript(OBJ:Val, I:Int) => applyIndex(OBJ, I) ... </k>
    36	
    37	  syntax Val ::= applyIndex(Val, Int) [function]
    38	  rule applyIndex(list(VS:ValSeq),  I:Int) => valSeqAt(VS, normIdx(I, vsLen(VS)))
    39	  rule applyIndex(tuple(VS:ValSeq), I:Int) => valSeqAt(VS, normIdx(I, vsLen(VS)))
    40	  rule applyIndex(str(IS:IntSeq),   I:Int)
    41	    => str(iCons(intSeqAt(IS, normIdx(I, isLen(IS))), .IntSeq))
    42	
    43	  // ==== Slice: obj[lo:hi:step] (list / str) — CPython slice.indices ==========
    44	  syntax KItem ::= #evalB(Bound) | "#toSome"
    45	                 | #slLo(Val, Bound, Bound)
    46	                 | #slHi(Val, OptInt, Bound)
    47	                 | #slStep(Val, OptInt, OptInt)
    48	
    49	  syntax OptInt ::= "noB" | someB(Int)
    50	  rule <k> #evalB(NoBound)  => noB ... </k>
    51	  rule <k> #evalB(E:Expr)   => E ~> #toSome ... </k>
    52	  rule <k> I:Int ~> #toSome => someB(I) ... </k>
    53	
    54	  rule <k> Subscript(OBJ:Val, Slice(LO:Bound, HI:Bound, ST:Bound)) => #evalB(LO) ~> #slLo(OBJ, HI, ST) ... </k>
    55	  rule <k> LO:OptInt ~> #slLo(OBJ:Val, HI:Bound, ST:Bound)   => #evalB(HI) ~> #slHi(OBJ, LO, ST) ... </k>
    56	  rule <k> HI:OptInt ~> #slHi(OBJ:Val, LO:OptInt, ST:Bound)  => #evalB(ST) ~> #slStep(OBJ, LO, HI) ... </k>
    57	  // a list slice constructs a NEW object; a str slice stays a value
    58	  rule <k> ST:OptInt ~> #slStep(list(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt)
    59	        => #alloc(doSlice(list(VS), LO, HI, ST)) ... </k>
    60	       [priority(45)]
    61	  rule <k> ST:OptInt ~> #slStep(OBJ:Val, LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt) => doSlice(OBJ, LO, HI, ST) ... </k>
    62	
    63	  syntax Val ::= doSlice(Val, OptInt, OptInt, OptInt) [function]
    64	  rule doSlice(list(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    65	    => list(buildVS(VS, slStart(LO, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStop(HI, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStep(ST)))
    66	  rule doSlice(tuple(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    67	    => tuple(buildVS(VS, slStart(LO, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStop(HI, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStep(ST)))
    68	  rule doSlice(str(IS:IntSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    69	    => str(buildIS(IS, slStart(LO, ST, isLen(IS)), slStop(HI, ST, isLen(IS)), slStep(ST)))
    70	
    71	  // ==== slice.indices: step / start / stop / clamp ==========================
    72	  syntax Int ::= slStep(OptInt) [function, total]
    73	  rule slStep(noB)          => 1
    74	  rule slStep(someB(S:Int)) => S
    75	
    76	  syntax Int ::= slStart(OptInt, OptInt, Int) [function]
    77	  rule slStart(noB,          ST:OptInt, _LEN:Int) => 0
    78	       requires slStep(ST) >Int 0
    79	  rule slStart(noB,          ST:OptInt, LEN:Int)  => LEN -Int 1
    80	       requires slStep(ST) <Int 0
    81	  rule slStart(someB(I:Int), ST:OptInt, LEN:Int)  => slAdjust(I, LEN, slStep(ST))
    82	
    83	  syntax Int ::= slStop(OptInt, OptInt, Int) [function]
    84	  rule slStop(noB,          ST:OptInt, LEN:Int)  => LEN
    85	       requires slStep(ST) >Int 0
    86	  rule slStop(noB,          ST:OptInt, _LEN:Int) => -1
    87	       requires slStep(ST) <Int 0
    88	  rule slStop(someB(I:Int), ST:OptInt, LEN:Int)  => slAdjust(I, LEN, slStep(ST))
    89	
    90	  syntax Int ::= slAdjust(Int, Int, Int) [function, total]
    91	  rule slAdjust(I:Int, LEN:Int, STEP:Int) => clampLo(I +Int LEN, STEP)
    92	       requires I  <Int 0
    93	  rule slAdjust(I:Int, LEN:Int, STEP:Int) => clampHi(I, LEN, STEP)
    94	       requires I >=Int 0
    95	
    96	  syntax Int ::= clampLo(Int, Int) [function, total]
    97	  rule clampLo(J:Int, _STEP:Int) => J
    98	       requires J >=Int 0
    99	  rule clampLo(J:Int, STEP:Int)  => #if STEP <Int 0 #then -1 #else 0 #fi
   100	       requires J <Int 0
   101	
   102	  syntax Int ::= clampHi(Int, Int, Int) [function, total]
   103	  rule clampHi(I:Int, LEN:Int, _STEP:Int) => I
   104	       requires I  <Int LEN
   105	  rule clampHi(I:Int, LEN:Int, STEP:Int)  => #if STEP <Int 0 #then LEN -Int 1 #else LEN #fi
   106	       requires I >=Int LEN
   107	
   108	  // ==== build the strided sub-sequence (indices in range by construction) ====
   109	  syntax ValSeq ::= buildVS(ValSeq, Int, Int, Int) [function]
   110	  rule buildVS(VS:ValSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int)
   111	    => vCons(valSeqAt(VS, I), buildVS(VS, I +Int STEP, STOP, STEP))
   112	       requires (STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP)
   113	  rule buildVS(_:ValSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int) => .ValSeq
   114	       requires notBool ((STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP))
   115	
   116	  syntax IntSeq ::= buildIS(IntSeq, Int, Int, Int) [function]
   117	  rule buildIS(IS:IntSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int)
   118	    => iCons(intSeqAt(IS, I), buildIS(IS, I +Int STEP, STOP, STEP))
   119	       requires (STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP)
   120	  rule buildIS(_:IntSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int) => .IntSeq
   121	       requires notBool ((STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP))
   122	endmodule
     1	// reference/src/semantics/operators.k — MPY-OPERATORS
     2	// The operator DISPATCH layer: operands evaluate by strictness (heat/cool over KResult=Val),
     3	// the cooled node hands to applyUn/applyBin/applyCmp (declared in core.k; each domain file
     4	// owns its cases — bool.k, int.k, float.k, str.k, list.k, tuple.k, set.k, dict.k).
     5	
     6	module MPY-OPERATORS
     7	  imports MPY-CORE
     8	  imports MPY-ITER
     9	
    10	  rule <k> UnaryOp(OP:String, V:Val) => applyUn(OP, V) ... </k>
    11	
    12	  rule <k> BinOp(OP:String, L:Val, R:Val) => applyBin(OP, L, R) ... </k>
    13	
    14	  // Compare's right operand sits under the CmpOp wrapper — contexts instead of attributes
    15	  context Compare(HOLE, _)
    16	  context Compare(_:Val, CmpOp(_, HOLE))
    17	  rule <k> Compare(LV:Val, CmpOp(OP:String, RV:Val)) => applyCmp(OP, LV, RV) ... </k> [owise]
    18	
    19	  rule applyCmp("is",     V:Val, noneV) => V ==K noneV
    20	  rule applyCmp("is not", V:Val, noneV) => notBool (V ==K noneV)
    21	
    22	  // ==== operand deref: heap objects combine/compare by STRUCTURE ============
    23	  // (Python: list == is structural; identity only via `is`.) priority(40)
    24	  // preempts the generic dispatch so applyUn/applyBin/applyCmp never see a ref.
    25	  rule <k> BinOp(OP:String, ref(H:Int), R:Expr) => BinOp(OP, V, R) ... </k>
    26	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    27	       [priority(40)]
    28	  rule <k> BinOp(OP:String, L:Val, ref(H:Int)) => BinOp(OP, L, V) ... </k>
    29	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    30	       requires notBool isRefV(L)
    31	       [priority(40)]
    32	
    33	  // the left operand of `in`/`not in` is an ELEMENT (compares by ==K) — never deref'd
    34	  rule <k> Compare(ref(H:Int), CmpOp(OP:String, R:Expr)) => Compare(V, CmpOp(OP, R)) ... </k>
    35	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    36	       requires OP =/=String "in" andBool OP =/=String "not in"
    37	       [priority(40)]
    38	  rule <k> Compare(L:Val, CmpOp(OP:String, ref(H:Int))) => Compare(L, CmpOp(OP, V)) ... </k>
    39	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    40	       requires notBool isRefV(L)
    41	        orBool OP ==String "in" orBool OP ==String "not in"
    42	       [priority(40)]
    43	
    44	  rule <k> UnaryOp(OP:String, ref(H:Int)) => UnaryOp(OP, V) ... </k>
    45	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    46	       [priority(40)]
    47	endmodule
     1	// reference/src/semantics/controls.k — MPY-CONTROLS
     2	
     3	module MPY-CONTROLS
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	  imports MPY-TUPLE
     6	  imports MPY-ITER
     7	
     8	  // ==== Assign / AugAssign (write the current scope; RHS evaluated by strictness) ==
     9	  rule <k> Assign(Name(X:String), V:Val) => .K ... </k>
    10	       <env> L:Int </env>
    11	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ X <- V ], _) ... </scopes>
    12	  rule <k> Assign(Name(X:String), V:Val) => #cellW({M[X]}:>Val, V) ... </k>
    13	       <env> L:Int </env>
    14	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    15	       requires "$cells" in_keys(M)
    16	        andBool pnMember(X, cellsOf({M["$cells"]}:>Val))
    17	        andBool X in_keys(M) andBool isCellRef({M[X]}:>Val)
    18	       [priority(40)]
    19	
    20	  rule <k> AugAssign(Name(X:String), OP:String, V:Val) => .K ... </k>
    21	       <env> L:Int </env>
    22	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ X <- applyBin(OP, {M[X]}:>Val, V) ], _) ... </scopes>
    23	       requires X in_keys(M)
    24	  // `lst += [..]` where lst is a heap ref: the generic rule leaves applyBin(OP, ref, V) — but the
    25	  // ref-deref preemption is BinOp-level (operators.k), so applyBin never derefs and it sticks. Route
    26	  // the ref case through BinOp so the deref + list-concat + #alloc path fires (result is a fresh ref).
    27	  rule <k> AugAssign(Name(X:String), OP:String, V:Val) => Assign(Name(X), BinOp(OP, Name(X), V)) ... </k>
    28	       <env> L:Int </env>
    29	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    30	       requires X in_keys(M) andBool isRefV({M[X]}:>Val)
    31	       [priority(40)]
    32	
    33	  // ==== import trivia: `from math import floor, ceil` binds the supported
    34	  // names as builtins in the current scope; every other import is a no-op
    35	  rule <k> ImportFrom("math", NS:ParamNames) => #bindImports(NS) ... </k>
    36	  rule <k> ImportFrom(_:String, _:ParamNames) => .K ... </k> [owise]
    37	  syntax KItem ::= #bindImports(ParamNames)
    38	  rule <k> #bindImports(.ParamNames) => .K ... </k>
    39	  rule <k> #bindImports((N:String, NS:ParamNames)) => #bindImports(NS) ... </k>
    40	       <env> L:Int </env>
    41	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ N <- builtinV(N) ], _) ... </scopes>
    42	       requires N ==String "floor" orBool N ==String "ceil"
    43	  rule <k> #bindImports((N:String, NS:ParamNames)) => #bindImports(NS) ... </k>
    44	       requires notBool (N ==String "floor" orBool N ==String "ceil")
    45	
    46	  // ==== Expr statement: evaluate for effect, discard the value ===============
    47	  // (bare calls — mutator methods, docstrings; the WP0 statement-trivia rung)
    48	  rule <k> Expr(_:Val) => .K ... </k>
    49	
    50	  // ==== If (condition evaluated by strictness) ==============================
    51	  syntax KItem ::= #branch(Bool, Stmts, Stmts)
    52	  rule <k> If(C:Val, T:Stmts, E:Stmts) => #branch(truthy(C), T, E) ... </k>
    53	  rule <k> #branch(true,  T:Stmts, _:Stmts) => T ... </k>
    54	  rule <k> #branch(false, _:Stmts, E:Stmts) => E ... </k>
    55	
    56	  // ==== IfExp: ternary T if C else E ========================================
    57	  rule <k> IfExp(V:Val, T:Expr, _:Expr) => T ... </k>
    58	       requires truthy(V)
    59	  rule <k> IfExp(V:Val, _:Expr, E:Expr) => E ... </k>
    60	       requires notBool truthy(V)
    61	
    62	  // ==== For: one loop, in-cell continuation, over #iterNext =================
    63	  // (the iterable is evaluated once, by strictness; the protocol stays rewrites —
    64	  // circularities anchor on #loop and narrowing substitutes the structure)
    65	  syntax KItem ::= #loop(Val, Expr, Stmts) | #loopStep(Expr, Stmts)
    66	                 | #while(Expr, Stmts) | #whileCond(Expr, Stmts)
    67	                 | #loopLbl(K) | "#cont" | "#brk"
    68	
    69	  rule <k> For(T:Expr, OBJ:Val, B:Stmts) => #loop(OBJ, T, B) ... </k>
    70	
    71	  rule <k> #loop(IT:Iterable, T:Expr, B:Stmts) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #loopStep(T, B) ... </k>
    72	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #loopStep(_:Expr, _:Stmts) => .K ... </k>
    73	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, REST:Iterable) ~> #loopStep(T:Expr, B:Stmts)
    74	        => #bindTgt(T, V) ~> B ~> #loopLbl(#loop(REST, T, B)) ... </k>
    75	
    76	  // ==== While ==============================================================
    77	  rule <k> While(C:Expr, B:Stmts) => #while(C, B) ... </k>
    78	  rule <k> #while(C:Expr, B:Stmts) => C ~> #whileCond(C, B) ... </k>
    79	  rule <k> V:Val ~> #whileCond(C:Expr, B:Stmts) => B ~> #loopLbl(#while(C, B)) ... </k>
    80	       requires truthy(V)
    81	  rule <k> V:Val ~> #whileCond(_C:Expr, _B:Stmts) => .K ... </k>
    82	       requires notBool truthy(V)
    83	
    84	  // ==== loop control (break / continue) =====================================
    85	  rule <k> #loopLbl(NEXT:K) => NEXT ... </k>
    86	  rule <k> Continue => #cont ... </k>
    87	  rule <k> Break => #brk ... </k>
    88	  rule <k> #cont ~> #loopLbl(NEXT:K) => NEXT ... </k>
    89	  rule <k> #cont ~> (_:KItem => .K) ... </k> [owise]
    90	  rule <k> #brk ~> #loopLbl(_:K) => .K ... </k>
    91	  rule <k> #brk ~> (_:KItem => .K) ... </k> [owise]
    92	
    93	  // ==== heap-object deref at the truthiness/iteration consumers ==============
    94	  // (priority(40) preempts the generic Val rules so truthy/#loop never see a ref)
    95	  rule <k> If(ref(H:Int), T:Stmts, E:Stmts) => If(V, T, E) ... </k>
    96	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    97	       [priority(40)]
    98	  rule <k> IfExp(ref(H:Int), T:Expr, E:Expr) => IfExp(V, T, E) ... </k>
    99	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
   100	       [priority(40)]
   101	  rule <k> ref(H:Int) ~> #whileCond(C:Expr, B:Stmts) => V ~> #whileCond(C, B) ... </k>
   102	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
   103	       [priority(40)]
   104	  // For derefs its iterable ONCE at loop start (iteration is over the snapshot;
   105	  // mutating the iterated list inside its own loop is outside the subset)
   106	  rule <k> For(T:Expr, ref(H:Int), B:Stmts) => For(T, V, B) ... </k>
   107	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
   108	       [priority(40)]
   109	endmodule
     1	// reference/src/semantics/iter.k — MPY-ITER
     2	// The iterator protocol, DECLARATION ONLY. Each iterable's #iterNext case lives in that
     3	// iterable's own module (list/tuple/str in their modules, rangeObj in range.k, zip in
     4	// builtins.k). Consumers (the for-loop, `x in _`, sum/all/any/max/min) import this.
     5	
     6	module MPY-ITER
     7	  imports MPY-CORE
     8	  syntax KItem ::= #iterNext(Iterable) | "#iterDone" | #iterYield(Val, Iterable)
     9	endmodule
     1	// reference/src/semantics/list.k — MPY-LIST
     2	
     3	module MPY-LIST
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	  imports MPY-ITER
     6	  imports MPY-OPERATORS
     7	
     8	  // ==== iteration (the iterator protocol's list case) =======================
     9	  rule <k> #iterNext(list(.ValSeq))                => #iterDone ... </k>
    10	  rule <k> #iterNext(list(vCons(V:Val, R:ValSeq))) => #iterYield(V, list(R)) ... </k>
    11	
    12	  // ==== ListExpr: [...] literal -> a fresh heap object =======================
    13	  syntax ApplyK ::= "toList"
    14	  rule <k> ListExpr(ES:Exprs) => #evalArgs(ES, .Vals, toList) ... </k>
    15	  rule <k> #applyK(toList, ACC:Vals) => #alloc(list(vals2valSeq(ACC))) ... </k>
    16	
    17	  // ==== list ops: + / == / != ===============================================
    18	  syntax ValSeq ::= valSeqConcat(ValSeq, ValSeq) [function, total]
    19	  rule valSeqConcat(.ValSeq, T:ValSeq)                => T
    20	  rule valSeqConcat(vCons(V:Val, S:ValSeq), T:ValSeq) => vCons(V, valSeqConcat(S, T))
    21	
    22	  // list + list constructs a NEW object (k-cell — it allocates; operands land here
    23	  // already deref'd). priority(45) beats the generic BinOp dispatch.
    24	  rule <k> BinOp("+", list(A:ValSeq), list(B:ValSeq)) => #alloc(list(valSeqConcat(A, B))) ... </k>
    25	       [priority(45)]
    26	
    27	  rule applyCmp("==", list(A:ValSeq), list(B:ValSeq)) => A ==K B
    28	  rule applyCmp("!=", list(A:ValSeq), list(B:ValSeq)) => notBool (A ==K B)

*** Add File: /audit-output/REVIEW.md
+# Independent adversarial audit: 146-specialFilter
+
+The candidate is **not a legitimate partial-correctness proof of the requested
+program over its intended integer-list domain**. Fresh reconstruction does
+produce `#Top` for both submitted claims, and the implementation agrees with
+the canonical Python function on the tested domain. Those facts do not rescue
+the proof: the only function-entry theorem is for the empty list, while the
+universal loop theorem replaces the result-bearing decimal computation with
+three unconstrained proof-local symbols that are reused in its postcondition.
+A fresh opposite-interpretation experiment proves a symbolic conclusion whose
+concrete `N = 12` instance is false.
+
+The rendered mode is `SUPPLIED_SEMANTICS`. The trusted mount is consistent with
+that mode, so this is a candidate verdict rather than an infrastructure error.
+
+## 1. Input and provenance integrity
+
+I treated every file below `/candidate` as untrusted and copied only source
+artifacts into fresh directories below `/tmp/audit-work`. I did not copy or use
+candidate compiled definitions or caches.
+
+The mode boundary passes. `/reference/reference-semantics` is a real directory.
+A recursive path/type/content comparison between it and
+`/candidate/reference-semantics` found zero differences. There are no missing,
+additional, changed, mistyped, or symlinked entries in the candidate semantics
+tree. The candidate `prompt.py` and `py2mpy.py` are regular files and byte-match
+their trusted versions:
+
+- prompt SHA-256:
+  `310a71d2feca4b63bf4ab0279cac60820a61a57157a413efd62823e6c69eb917`
+- translator SHA-256:
+  `406485eac118431c08ef59f30f79dfa6aa9d5825408917fc5ce7c806e664db16`
+
+The required source files `solution.py`, `solution.mpy`, `spec.k`, and
+`verification.k` are regular files, not symlinks. No source-type defect was
+found.
+
+The requested provenance records are all missing:
+
+- `/candidate/run-input.json`
+- `/candidate/metrics.json`
+- `/candidate/codex-last.txt`
+- `/candidate/codex-output.log`
+
+No structured generation trace is present. `PROOF.md` is also absent. The
+candidate does contain untrusted `call-proof.out` and `loop-proof.out` files,
+each containing only `#Top`, plus `concrete-krun.out`; none was relied on.
+
+Evidence: [integrity script](/audit-output/evidence/stage1_integrity.sh) and
+[bounded log](/audit-output/evidence/stage1_integrity.log).
+
+## 2. Program fidelity and candidate-versus-canonical checks
+
+The trusted prompt requires counting array elements that:
+
+1. are greater than 10; and
+2. have odd first and last digits in their ordinary decimal representation.
+
+The trusted canonical implementation iterates over `nums`, converts each
+qualifying number with `str`, converts its first and last characters to
+integers, and tests membership in `(1, 3, 5, 7, 9)`. The candidate uses direct
+character membership in `"13579"`. For positive integers, these tests are
+equivalent.
+
+Trusted retranslation of the scratch copy of `solution.py` exited 0 and was
+byte-identical to submitted `solution.mpy`; both have SHA-256
+`d3d8c79a12490216fd14e7573efbd7abb0031ed6ae1ae9e4bd8a269df68ff113`.
+
+I independently loaded `/reference/canonical.py` and `/candidate/solution.py`
+with bytecode writes disabled. The deterministic corpus included both
+documented examples, the empty list, threshold values 9/10/11, first- and
+last-digit branch combinations, negative values, large integers, every
+singleton from -250 through 400, all pairs from a 25-value branch-boundary
+set, and 1,000 seeded generated lists. Results:
+
+- domain tested: finite lists of Python integers
+- cases: 2,289
+- mismatches: 0
+- complete-input SHA-256:
+  `54f046ad18798f63707bb7a5e3492e320a5ddf4e0f270c7a902eb3a6bc7158c4`
+
+In particular, both Python functions return 0 for `[12]`, 1 for `[15]`, 2 for
+`[12, 15, 33]`, and 0 for `[]`.
+
+The K proof formalizes only finite integer lists. The prompt says “numbers,”
+but its digit operation and the supplied task context support the integer
+reading; non-integer numeric inputs remain outside the formal theorem.
+
+Evidence: [fidelity script](/audit-output/evidence/stage2_fidelity.sh),
+[fidelity log](/audit-output/evidence/stage2_fidelity.log),
+[differential source](/audit-output/evidence/differential_test.py), and
+[complete inputs](/audit-output/evidence/differential-inputs.json).
+
+## 3. Clean proof reconstruction
+
+I used K v7.1.337. The final clean rerun used
+`/tmp/audit-work/candidate-clean-rerun`, containing only copied candidate
+sources and the integrity-checked supplied semantics. It contained no
+candidate definition or cache.
+
+The reconstruction script records the exact commands. Results were:
+
+| Operation | Exit | Required result |
+|---|---:|---|
+| Trusted translation of reviewer concrete test | 0 | generated `.mpy` |
+| LLVM `MPY-KRUN` build | 0 | fresh `runtime-kompiled` |
+| Reviewer concrete `krun` | 0 | final `NoExc` |

used to prove the loop claim.

### False-conclusion witness for the decimal bridges

The complete match domain of the three bridges is any occurrence of:

- `strToCodes(Int2String(N))`;
- `isLen(decimalCodes(N))`;
- `intSeqAt(decimalCodes(N), I)`.

They affect the value assigned to `digits`, the two membership branches,
`count`, `specialCount`, `finalDigits`, and the final loop postcondition. Their
only claimed support is that execution and contract use the same symbols,
which is circular.

I supplied a consistent opposite interpretation allowed by those symbols:
every symbolic integer has decimal length 2 and every projected character is
ASCII 49 (`'1'`). In a definition that imports the candidate proof syntax but
not its loop-summary rule, `kprove` directly executes the actual element body
and proves `#Top` for the symbolic claim “every `N > 10` increments count.”
The concrete instance `N = 12` is false: both Python implementations return 0
for `[12]`.

A separate ground attempt did not use the symbolic bridge: the fixed hook
reduced 12 to codes 49,50, the body produced count 0, and the false count-1
claim became stuck. This contrast is the witness: the symbolic bridge admits a
universal conclusion whose ground fixed-semantics instance disagrees.

The independent body-sensitivity mutation changed `count += 1` to
`count += 2`. Its definition built, and the original loop obligation failed
with the expected residual comparing `C + 2 + specialCount(REST)` against
`C + (specialCount(REST) + 1)`. This supports control/body fidelity but does
not repair the decimal-value oracle.

Evidence: [mutation patch](/audit-output/evidence/body-mutation.patch),
[script](/audit-output/evidence/stage5_body_sensitivity.sh), and

## 6. Fresh non-vacuity test

The candidate has no `spec-vacuity.k`. I created a new claim with the same
satisfiable empty-call precondition but changed the required return from 0 to
1.

The mutation parsed and built to KORE under `kprove --dry-run` with exit 0.
The actual proof exited 1 with `WarnStuckClaimState`; its reachable residual
contains `0 ~> .K`, while the destination requires 1, followed by the expected
“cannot be rewritten further” prover error. The failure is therefore the
intended unmet result obligation, not a parser, import, timeout, or unrelated
backend failure.

This establishes non-vacuity of the narrow empty-input result constraint. It
does not establish universal entry coverage and does not validate the opaque
loop result.

Evidence: [false spec](/audit-output/evidence/spec-vacuity.k),
[non-vacuity script](/audit-output/evidence/stage6_nonvacuity.sh),
[dry-run log](/audit-output/evidence/stage6_vacuity_dry_run.log), and
[stuck proof log](/audit-output/evidence/stage6_vacuity_proof.log).

## 7. Proven versus assumed accounting

Under the supplied semantics plus all candidate proof extensions, the two
successful reachability proofs establish exactly:

- an arbitrary-length internal loop transforms the named local variables
  according to `specialCount`, `finalNum`, and `finalDigits`; and
- a directly constructed exact-body closure returns 0 on the empty synthetic
  integer list and restores the stated call state.

They do not establish a universal call theorem for `specialFilter`, do not
execute the submitted module in an entry claim, and do not establish that
`specialCount` is the count of standard-decimal odd-ended integers.

The trust ledger is:

| Boundary | Influence and dependents | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Byte-identical supplied semantics | All execution and both claims | Accepted fixed semantics by the rendered mode. |
| Trusted `py2mpy.py` | Python-to-`.mpy` program identity | Accepted; byte identity independently checked. |
| K v7.1.337 toolchain/backend | Builds and reachability closure | Normal proof-system trust boundary. |
| `intVals` representation and iterator rules | Universal integer-list loop | Acceptable typed representation; exact base/cons behavior. |
| Three opaque decimal symbols and simplification bridges | String value, indexing, membership branches, `specialBit`, `specialCount`, loop summary | Illegitimate program-derived oracle. No bridge-free connection theorem; false symbolic conclusion witnessed. |
| Priority loop summary | Empty call proof and any future caller proof | Exact context and body-sensitive, but justified only under the illegitimate decimal theory. |
| Python differential corpus | Implementation-to-canonical bridge on 2,289 integer-list cases | Useful finite evidence only; not a universal K theorem. |
| Standard-decimal interpretation of opaque symbols | Human-facing meaning of the loop postcondition | Merely informal/empirical; absent from the formal theory. |
| Termination | All reachability conclusions | Not proved; ordinary partial-correctness limitation. |

Gate assessment:

- Dynamic reconstruction: **PASS** (`#Top` for both claims).
- Real-program soundness/result-bearing abstraction: **FAIL**.
- Intent adequacy/universal entry pinning: **FAIL**.
- Evidence auditability: **limited** by missing generation records, though the
  independent evidence produced here is reproducible.
- Fresh narrow-claim non-vacuity: **PASS**.

The material failures meet the decision boundary for `FAIL / NOT_LEGIT`: the
proof covers only an empty end-to-end call and relies on a result-bearing,
unconstrained oracle chain for its universal internal result.

VERDICT: FAIL
LEGITIMACY: NOT_LEGIT
